summary.text: A river delta is a landform, usually triangular, built from sediment a river drops where it meets slow-moving or still water such as a sea, lake or reservoir.
Entering open water, the flow spreads out and slows, so it can no longer carry its load and the sediment settles to build up the delta.
Deltas are major farming and population centers, can defend coastlines, and over geologic time act as important carbon sinks.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Greek capital delta (Δ), after the Nile Delta's shape

facts.label: First English use
facts.value: Late 18th century, in the work of Edward Gibbon

facts.label: Herodotus
facts.value: Mentions the Delta fourteen times in his Histories

items.prompt: A muddy river pours into a calm lake. Why does it drop most of its mud right near the mouth?

options.label: Lake water is colder and makes mud clump
Fish and plants filter the mud out at once
The flow spreads out, slows and can't carry it
The lake bed pulls sediment down like a magnet

items.explain: Freed from its channel, the flow widens and slows, losing its ability to transport sediment, which settles out.

items.prompt: Where does the word 'delta' for a river mouth landform come from?

options.label: An ancient Greek word for mud
The shape of a Greek capital letter
The fourth river the Greeks mapped
A Roman god of rivers and floods

items.explain: The Nile Delta's triangular shape resembles the uppercase Greek letter delta, Δ.

items.prompt: As a delta grows seaward, its channel gets longer while dropping the same height, so it silts up and its bed rises. What tends to happen next?

options.label: The river dries up completely
The channel cuts deeper and stays put
The delta stops growing for good
It breaks out onto a shorter, steeper course

items.explain: The lower gradient destabilizes the channel; when the river breaches its levees, such as in a flood, it takes a shorter, steeper route.

items.prompt: One river switches its course across its delta very often; another rarely does. Which delta ends up shaped most like a smooth, even fan?

options.label: The one that switches course often
The one that rarely switches course
Both end up as identical fans
Neither, as switching makes no difference

items.explain: More frequent channel changes spread sediment more evenly, so the shape gets closer to an ideal fan; rarely switching rivers like the Mississippi form bird's feet.

items.prompt: A river reaches a coast where the seafloor plunges into a steep subduction trench. Compared with a river on a broad, gentle shelf, what happens to its sediment?

options.label: It builds an even bigger delta than usual
It piles up in a tall underwater mountain
It flows back upstream with the tides
It slides into the trench instead of piling up

items.explain: On steep active margins, sediment travels into the trench rather than accumulating on a shallow shelf, so large deltas rarely form.

items.prompt: A bar of sand and gravel settles in the middle of a river mouth. How does it change the river?

options.label: Water routes around it and splits into two channels
Water backs up behind it and forms a lake
Water washes it away within a single day
Water speeds up and digs a single deep channel

items.explain: Flow goes around a mouth bar, more sediment builds on its upstream end, and the river divides into two distributary channels.

paragraphs.heading: Land built by a river
paragraphs.text: A river delta is a landform, often triangular, built from sediment that a river drops where it meets slow-moving or still water. That water can be an ocean, sea, estuary, lake or reservoir, or more rarely another river that cannot carry the sediment away. The name comes from the capital Greek letter delta (Δ), because the Nile Delta is roughly that shape.

paragraphs.heading: Why the sediment drops
paragraphs.text: A delta begins when a river carrying sediment enters standing water. Freed from its channel, the flow spreads sideways, and as it widens it slows down. Slower water can carry less sediment, so the load settles out as alluvium and builds up into the delta. Over time a single channel builds a lobe of new land and pushes its mouth further out, as in the bird's-foot shape of the Mississippi and Ural deltas.

paragraphs.heading: Rivers that switch course
paragraphs.text: As the lobe grows, the channel gets longer without dropping any further, so its slope becomes gentler. A gentler slope means less force on the riverbed, so sediment settles inside the channel and the bed rises compared with the floodplain, which makes the channel unstable. If the river breaks through its natural levees, for example in a flood, it takes a new, shorter route to the sea with a steeper, steadier slope. Some water usually keeps flowing down the old channel, and repeated switches build a mature delta with a branching network of channels.

paragraphs.heading: Bars, branches and fans
paragraphs.text: Branches can also start at mouth bars, which are sand or gravel bars dropped in the middle of a river's mouth. The water flows around the bar, more sediment piles up on its upstream end, and the river splits into two channels; the Wax Lake Delta shows this well. Because shifting channels spread sediment across the surface, many deltas take on a fan shape, and the more often the river changes course, the closer that shape gets to an ideal fan. The Mississippi and Ural deltas, with their bird's-foot outlines, switch too rarely to make a symmetrical fan.

paragraphs.heading: Why deltas matter
paragraphs.text: Deltas are major centers of farming and population, which makes them important to human civilization. They can help defend coastlines and can affect drinking water supplies. They are also ecologically important, with different groups of species depending on where in the landscape they sit. Over geologic time they are important carbon sinks as well.

paragraphs.heading: Where big deltas form
paragraphs.text: Most large deltas, including those of the Mississippi, Nile, Amazon, Ganges, Indus, Yangtze and Yellow rivers, lie along passive continental margins. There the land slopes gently over a wide area, so sediment can pile up over time into big deltas. Along active margins the slopes are steeper and narrower, and sediment tends to run into a steep subduction trench instead of building up on a shallow continental shelf.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient name
paragraphs.text: The triangle was noticed early. Aeschylus's tragedy Prometheus Bound calls the Nile region the triangular Nilotic land, and Herodotus's Histories mentions the Delta fourteen times, describing silt flowing out into the sea. According to Strabo, Onesicritus, who travelled with Alexander the Great, called the land at the mouth of the Indus a delta. As a general English word for this landform, delta first turns up in the late 18th century, in the writing of Edward Gibbon.
